examples.problem_statement: Churchill conceded that Russia, (i) _________ an ally of France and Great Britain, was in fact (ii) _________ to their security, but argued that Russian national interest would compel it to make (iii) _________ with those countries. Blank (i): steadfastly / nominally / sporadically. Blank (ii): pledged / indifferent / immune. Blank (iii): common cause / rack and ruin / vim and vigor.

solution.operation: Read the pivot phrase "in fact" joining the first two blanks
solution.result: Russia did not show the concern for French and British security that an ally would be expected to show
solution.description: Locate the phrase "in fact" and use it to set the direction of the sentence: it flags that Russia's real stance falls short of what its ally status implies.

solution.operation: For blank (i), require a word describing an ally that is not fully committed
solution.description: Choose the blank (i) word from the requirement set in step 1 - the word must qualify "ally" as incomplete, and "nominally" does exactly that by making the alliance one of name alone.

solution.operation: For blank (ii), require a word meaning "not concerned"
solution.description: Fill blank (ii) with the word matching the meaning "not concerned": "indifferent" says Russia did not really care about their security.

solution.operation: Read the "but" that introduces the final clause
solution.result: Churchill argued Russia would nevertheless act as an ally, for its own national reasons
solution.description: Use the contrast word "but" to reverse direction for the last clause: despite the indifference just established, Russia is predicted to behave as an ally.

solution.operation: For blank (iii), require an idiom meaning "to act as an ally"
solution.description: Select the blank (iii) phrase that carries the acting-as-an-ally meaning established in step 4 - to make common cause is to act as an ally.

key_reminders: "In fact" signals that the reality contradicts the label just applied.
"But" reverses the direction of the clause it introduces.
"Nominally" means in name only; "to make common cause" means to act as an ally.
common_mistakes: Choosing "steadfastly" for blank (i), which agrees with "ally" instead of setting up the contrast that "in fact" demands.
Reading the final "but" as continuing the indifference, which pushes blank (iii) toward a hostile phrase rather than an allied one.

concept.technique_name: plugging in values to test a comparison
concept.sub_category: Quantitative Comparison with a linear equation

examples.problem_statement: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B, given x + y = -1. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: y. Choose: (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: x = 0, y = -1, so x is greater than y
solution.description: Plug an easy value into one variable and read off the other: setting x to 0 forces y to -1, and this pair makes Quantity A the larger one.

solution.result: y = 0, x = -1, so y is greater than x
solution.description: Repeat the plug-in with the roles swapped: setting y to 0 forces x to -1, and now Quantity B is the larger one.

solution.result: y expressed directly in terms of x
solution.description: Solve the constraint for y so that any chosen x immediately gives its matching y, which makes further testing quicker.

solution.result: y < 0, so x is greater than y for every positive x
solution.description: Read the rewritten equation for positive x: the minus sign in front of x drives y below zero, so Quantity A wins on this whole range.

solution.result: y > 0, so y is greater than x on that range
solution.description: Read the same equation for x below -1: now -x - 1 comes out positive, so Quantity B wins on this range.

solution.operation: Compare the two ranges of outcomes found in steps 4 and 5
solution.result: Both orderings occur among pairs satisfying the equation, so no fixed relationship exists
solution.description: Collect the conflicting results: because some valid pairs make x larger and others make y larger, the comparison cannot be settled from the given information.

examples.answer: Choice D: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

key_reminders: A single equation in two variables leaves infinitely many valid pairs, so one test case never settles a comparison.
Two test cases that give opposite orderings are enough to prove the relationship cannot be determined.
Solving for one variable (y = -x - 1) makes it easy to scan whole ranges of x at once.
common_mistakes: Stopping after the single pair x = 0, y = -1 and concluding Quantity A is greater.
Testing only positive values of x, which hides the x < -1 range where y becomes greater.

examples.problem_statement: The cost of a certain commodity is expressed by the formula tb^4, where t and b are both greater than 0. If b is doubled, by what factor will the cost of the commodity increase? (A) 2 (B) 6 (C) 8 (D) 16

solution.result: a concrete starting value for b
solution.description: Pick an easy number for the variable being doubled so the two costs can be compared numerically rather than symbolically.
Evaluate the cost formula at the picked value: with b = 1 the fourth power contributes nothing and the cost is just t.

solution.operation: Double b to 2, then t b^4 = t \cdot 2^4
solution.description: Apply the doubling to the picked value and re-evaluate the same formula: raising 2 to the fourth power gives 16, so the cost becomes 16t.
Divide the new cost by the original cost to read off the factor of increase, which is 16.

key_reminders: Picking a convenient value such as b = 1 is legitimate here because the answer is a ratio and t cancels.
Doubling a quantity raised to the fourth power multiplies the result by 2^4, not by 2.
common_mistakes: Answering 8 by treating the exponent as a cube, or 2 by ignoring the exponent entirely.
Multiplying the exponent instead of raising the doubling factor to it (4 x 2 = 8 rather than 2^4 = 16).

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. "As my eyesight began to ______, I spent a lot of time writing about it - both poems and 'eye journals' - describing what I saw as I looked out through damaged eyes." A deteriorate B sharpen C improve D decline E recover F adjust

solution.operation: Take the clue "damaged eyes" from the end of the sentence
solution.result: the blank must express eyesight getting worse
solution.description: Anchor the blank to the fact stated later in the sentence: the eyes are damaged, so whatever fills the blank has to reflect that.

solution.result: both fit the damaged-eyes clue and yield sentences alike in meaning
solution.description: Check the two worsening words: each one makes sense in the blank and the two completed sentences say the same thing, which is what this question type demands.

solution.result: alike in meaning as a pair, but contradict the damaged-eyes clue
solution.description: Examine this rival pair: they do match each other, but they fail the sentence sense from step 1, so a matching pair alone is not enough.

solution.result: makes some sense but has no partner among the remaining choices
solution.description: Check the leftover plausible word: even though it can be read into the blank, no other option produces a sentence similar in meaning to it, so it cannot be part of the answer.

solution.operation: Keep the only pair that satisfies both requirements
solution.description: Combine the two tests - fits the sentence and forms an alike-in-meaning pair - and select deteriorate and decline.

examples.answer: Choice A: deteriorate; AND Choice D: decline

key_reminders: The two correct choices must both fit the sentence and produce completed sentences alike in meaning.
A word that fits the sentence but has no synonym among the choices cannot be correct.
A synonym pair that contradicts the sentence's own evidence is a trap, not an answer.
common_mistakes: Picking "sharpen" and "improve" because they pair with each other, ignoring the "damaged eyes" clue.
Selecting "adjust" on plausibility alone even though no partner word matches it.
